newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakh reformist PM plays down fears of sacking.
newsitem.headline: Kazakh reformist PM plays down fears of sacking.

text.p: Kazakhstan's reformist Prime Minister Akezhan Kazhegeldin, under fire from President Nursultan Nazarbayev over unpaid wages, on Wednesday played down fears that he was about to lose his job.

Earlier this week Nazarbayev sent jitters through the foreign investment community in the resource-rich former Soviet republic when he threatened Kazhegeldin with the sack over wage and pension arrears.
"I consider that first I must fulfil my duty and my word, which I gave to my people and my president," Kazhegeldin told a news conference, adding that he had not been asked to resign.
But he made clear he would have no problem finding other work if Nazarbayev dropped him, saying he had received offers from a range of European financial institutes to work as a consultant.
"If in the end I am freed from my duties then I shall definitely make the most of the opportunity and help Western financial institutes to get into the Kazakh market," he added.

Kazhegeldin, 45, a successful businessman before his appointment as prime minister in October 1994, is seen by Western investors as the main guarantor of market economic reforms in the vast Central Asian nation.
Rumours of his imminent sacking have been circulating in the Kazakh capital Almaty for weeks.
Observers say Nazarbayev, who enjoys strong executive powers, is concerned about his growing unpopularity among the 16.9 million population over wages and pensions, which have gone unpaid for months.
He gave Kazhegeldin until April 10 to resolve the problem.
Nazarbayev's ultimatum came as Kazhegeldin waged a high-stakes political battle over the multi-billion dollar privatisation of the country's oil and gas industry.
Kazhegeldin favours participation of Western investors in the process while the republic's Soviet-era directors do not.
